It comprises a catalytically inactive Cas9 protein bound to a single-guide RNA, which directs the complex to a specific genomic target sequence. The model also includes the catalytic core of the human acetyltransferase p300 and the target DNA.

Once recruited to the target site, the p300 catalytic domain promotes acetylation of histone H3 at lysine 27 (H3K27ac), an epigenetic mark associated with active regulatory regions and increased gene expression.

The model was developed for a nonprofit scientific animation project exploring the CRISPR–Cas system and its potential applications. The animation was created for educational and scientific communication purposes and was endorsed for its "stunning imagery and attention to detail" by Dr. Jennifer A. Doudna and Dr. Emmanuelle Charpentier, recipients of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the development of a method for genome editing.

The project was conducted under the supervision of Dr. Ramiro Esteban Rodriguez Virasoro at the Cell Biology of Plant Development Laboratory, Instituto de Biología Molecular y Celular de Rosario (IBR–CONICET).

The device was developed to grow Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings while mounting them directly onto a microscopy coverslip, enabling confocal live-cell imaging without manipulating or disturbing the roots. This configuration allowed continuous observation of living root cells under physiologically relevant conditions.

This design better mimics the natural growth environment of seedlings, in which roots remain underground and aerial tissues are exposed to illumination.
